title: Two Ways to Split
question: How can one cell divide in two different ways for two different jobs?
hook: A cell can split into identical copies or into cells with half the chromosomes, and each way has its own job.
idea: Mitosis makes genetically identical cells with the chromosome number kept, while meiosis makes four haploid cells, so the two do different jobs.

beats.prompt: A diploid cell, with two of each type of chromosome, goes through the vegetative division. What do its daughter cells look like?

choices.label: Genetically identical to the parent, with the same chromosome number
Haploid, with one of each type of chromosome
choices.feedback: That describes the division that makes gametes, not the vegetative one.

choices.label: A random mix, with a changed chromosome number
choices.feedback: The vegetative division keeps the total number of chromosomes the same.

beats.explain: Mitosis produces daughter cells genetically identical to the parent cell, with the total number of chromosomes maintained.

beats.prompt: Match each type of division to what it does.
beats.explain: Each division type has its own result, from identical copies to gametes to a whole new single-celled organism.

beats.prompt: Put the steps of meiosis in order.
beats.explain: Meiosis follows DNA replication with two divisions, ending in four haploid daughter cells.

beats.prompt: Sort each description into the division it fits.
items: Daughter cells genetically identical to the parent
beats.explain: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number and makes identical cells, while meiosis reduces it and makes haploid cells.
